default.p.test-1-p1.vietnamese: When we think of volunteering, it can be described as contribution carried out freely and in good faith. However, in recent years, there has been a reality far removed from this image of volunteering. Consider money, for example. In principle, volunteers do not receive compensation, but precisely because there is no compensation, it is difficult to attract people. Since expenses such as surcharges, transportation, gasoline, and food and lodging must be paid by the volunteers themselves, it becomes difficult to continue for a long time. In addition, the attitudes and behavior of people who come to volunteer are also considered a problem. Some are encouraged or even forced by their schools to volunteer; some do it to gain extra points for self-promotion when applying for jobs; and others have impure motives, such as trying to find themselves or wanting others to thank them. For these reasons, and also from the perspective of securing enough workers, shouldn't we broaden the definition of volunteering and also accept volunteer activities that are not entirely unpaid?

My wish to have a cat in my home is similar to my wish to have a dog happily running after me through fields or along streets. Dogs and cats are always around me, and what I want to write about here is precisely these dogs and cats. Realist friends advise me to publish separate books about dogs and cats because people who like dogs usually hate cats, while people who like cats hate dogs.

default.p.test-12-p1.vietnamese:
It is an international civilian volunteer organization dedicated to providing medical aid and protecting human rights across national borders for people suffering from disasters caused by armed conflict, natural disasters, or famine.

The organization was founded in 1971 in Paris, the capital of France, by doctors who had participated in famine relief efforts in Biafra in 1968.

Today, the organization has sections in 18 countries and secretariat offices in 2 countries around the world. Five of these locations—France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Spain—serve as operational sections, with a structure dedicated to forming teams of doctors and planning medical aid programs.

In 1999, the organization's 28 years of humanitarian aid activities were highly acclaimed, and it was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

default.p.test-17-p1.vietnamese:
When discussing organ transplantation, the unavoidable issue is brain death. First, the difference between brain death and ordinary death is as follows. Until now, a person was judged to be dead when all three conditions were met: the heart had stopped beating, breathing had stopped, and the pupils were dilated (the pupils were wide open and did not react to light). In contrast, in the case of brain death, a person is judged to have died when brain functions have stopped, even if the heart and breathing have not yet stopped. Even while connected to a ventilator, still breathing and with the heart still beating, the patient is declared dead. Under the previous criteria, the only organs that could be transplanted were the corneas and kidneys, but in cases of brain death, heart transplantation also became possible because the heart had not yet stopped functioning.

(One section omitted)

Organ donation is limited to people aged 15 or older who, while alive, expressed their willingness to undergo a brain-death diagnosis and consented to organ donation. In addition, it is essential that the family does not object to the transplantation.

The reason the minimum age is 15 is that, under the Civil Code, a will is considered legally valid from the age of 15. However, this means that organ donation by young children cannot be carried out. This is because large organs from an adult cannot be transplanted into a child's body. Whether the age of 15 is appropriate will probably continue to be debated in the future. In addition, because organ donation following brain death requires the donor's own wishes to have been expressed while alive, Organ Donor Intention Cards have recently begun to be distributed widely. By filling in the information, signing the card, and carrying it, people can confirm that they wish to donate their organs. The cards are available at city offices, health centers, post offices, driver's license testing centers, and some convenience stores.

default.p.test-18-p1.outline.3.label: A call for research on post-ethnic multiculturalism
default.p.test-18-p1.outline.3.note: Points toward the future: opening ourselves to cultural differences and beginning research into post-ethnic multiculturalism.
default.p.test-18-p1.vietnamese:
At the end of 2008, the number of foreign nationals registered as residents in Japan was approximately 2.3 million, exceeding about 1.7% of the total population. This figure was expected to continue increasing rapidly. The sharp increase in foreign residents and their long-term settlement represented an unprecedented situation for Japanese society in terms of the broad geographical scope, social backgrounds, and diversity of reasons for coming to Japan. Among these reasons, some people seek self-fulfillment, leaving the country where they were born and raised to test themselves in a broader world and challenge their potential; others may be described as a refugee type, seeking to escape economic, social, and psychological circumstances in their home countries. In either case, Japanese society is now facing the question of how to "live together" with foreign residents.

Until now, research in Japan has devoted considerable effort to collecting information from abroad and sending people overseas in pursuit of "outward-looking internationalization," but it has shown little interest in "internal internationalization." It seems that there has basically been a lack of an attitude that reexamines the reality right before us by looking at the people around us and learning from them.

From now on, if Japanese people wish to choose a way of life supported by multilingualism and multiculturalism, open their hearts to people with different linguistic backgrounds, ways of life, and values, accept those differences, and work toward living together, then it is entirely essential to begin research aimed at post-ethnic multiculturalism—one that is not narrowly bound by nationality or ethnicity alone.

default.p.test-19-p1.vietnamese:
As the proverb says, “A distant relative is less useful than a nearby neighbor,” relationships with neighbors are especially important. When children or grandchildren living far away become ill, the first people they seek help from are the neighbors around them. Thinking of this, parents must feel deeply grateful for the kindness of the neighbors of their sons and daughters.

On the other hand, people also often say, “Blood is thicker than water.” This means that no matter how kindly outsiders treat us, when we face prolonged trouble, it is ultimately our blood relatives who step forward to care for us and shoulder the burden.

(One section omitted)

Even with distant relatives, such as second cousins or cousins we have never met, for some reason we may still feel a surge of affection and nostalgia simply because they resemble someone familiar.

For that reason, in our relationships with outsiders, we should behave without becoming overly intimate or interfering deeply in other people's private lives, while still treating one another with warmth. People often say that a pawnbroker cannot have a close relationship with a customer. The same is said of a doctor treating patients for intimate illnesses: once the illness is cured, the relationship ends with a “Yes, all right, goodbye.” Even among very close friends, if one person suffers a misfortune and the other helps so enthusiastically that it goes beyond what even a blood relative would do, the relationship may become distant and awkward as a result. The saying “Lend money to a close friend and you lose both the money and the friend” describes a similarly difficult situation.

The saying “No matter how close you are, you must still observe proper etiquette” applies to families as well, and is this not the fundamental basis of all human relationships?

default.p.test-2-p1.outline.2.label: The burden on younger generations and recommendations for policy improvement

default.p.test-2-p1.vietnamese: In Japan, there has long been a belief that “caregiving is something that families must do at home.” In addition, as medical care continues to advance, the number of people requiring care is increasing, and the period during which care is needed is becoming longer. Despite needing care, some people are unable to receive adequate support. There is also a growing phenomenon known as “elderly caregiving for the elderly,” in which people aged 65 and over care for other elderly people. As a result, the burden of caregiving is extremely heavy, and in many cases this leads to elder abuse. This includes not only violence but also neglect, contempt, and the improper use of the victim’s assets. Because of the declining birth rate, the caregiving burden on younger people will likely become even heavier. The authorities must take this reality seriously and improve caregiving support policies.

default.p.test-20-p1.vietnamese:
In the United States, the number of “convenient care clinics” is rapidly increasing. These clinics are hired by pharmacy chains to provide medical services to patients who do not want to wait a long time at a hospital. Advanced-practice nurses can diagnose simple illnesses such as colds and prescribe medication there.

With only limited supervision, such as oversight by an internist, and the slogan “fast and inexpensive” as their selling point, these clinics have rapidly spread nationwide—from several dozen locations three or four years ago to 1,200 today. Some clinics have even managed to obtain larger supplies of scarce flu vaccines than the doctors in town, causing local residents to line up in long queues.

Although this seems to show the vitality of the American-style market economy, some people are concerned: “Can we really be sure that pharmacies are not pressuring them to prescribe too much medication?” This spring, one major clinic chain closed 90 of its 550 branches until the beginning of October, claiming only that it was the low-demand season. Howard Strom, a 60-year-old internist in Los Angeles, criticized them harshly: “They are doing it purely to make money.”

At a time when the United States is burdened with 46 million people without health insurance, Congress is at the center of a heated debate over reforming a healthcare safety net that has been left largely in private hands. It is understandable that the country traditionally values market forces, but should healthcare not fundamentally begin with people’s sense of security?

default.p.test-21-p1.vietnamese:
To vote in national elections from abroad, you must register on the overseas voter list. I am currently living in Los Angeles on a work assignment, but I was unable to vote in the House of Representatives election last August because I had not registered. It takes about two months from submitting the application to completing registration. By the time I realized it just before the election, it was too late.

It has been 10 years since this system was implemented. The estimated number of eligible voters worldwide is about 810,000, but the actual turnout in general elections is only slightly over 3%. Polling stations are limited to overseas diplomatic missions, while voting by mail involves complicated procedures and seems to be regarded by many people as a nuisance.

The local consulate estimates that the cost per ballot is about 70 dollars (approximately 6,300 yen), including media publicity, temporary staff wages, and the cost of transporting completed ballots to Japan.

If people could vote electronically over the Internet, even those living in remote areas could vote easily, and costs could also be reduced. The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications is cautious, saying that “security challenges still remain,” but Professor Shigeo Tsujii of Chuo University points out, “Technically, it is entirely feasible; the key issue is simply whether there is the determination to do it.”

Rather than saying, “Let’s try it in local elections first,” I sincerely hope that online voting will be introduced immediately in overseas elections, where the need is especially great.

default.p.test-22-p1.outline.1.note: Analyzes the early stage: technology came before purpose, and pioneers only needed to prove that they could photograph and “freeze” the natural world. Provides the basis for Questions 1 and 3.
default.p.test-22-p1.outline.2.label: The later stage: expanding the scope and subjects of observation
default.p.test-22-p1.outline.2.note: Describes the shift after novelty wears off: photography adopts a completely different method to broaden people’s horizons, allowing them to view distant landmarks such as the pyramids and images of people living at the time. Evidence for Question 2.
default.p.test-22-p1.vietnamese:
Today, with cameras and consumer photography becoming widespread so quickly, it may be difficult to imagine a world without photography. We grow up surrounded by photographs, and taking or looking at pictures has become part of everyday life. However, it is important to remember that photographic technology was once something new, filled with wonder and surprise. Once photographic technology had been perfected, how was this exciting medium ultimately put to use?

In the case of photography, it seems that technology came before its purpose. For ① the early pioneers, simply demonstrating in practice that photographic technology worked and could “freeze” the natural world was enough. Apart from reflecting the world as it was, the photographs taken by these pioneers also taught us many things about the world.

However, once its novelty had worn off, photographic technology began expanding the scope of human vision in ② a completely different way from before. Thanks to photography, people became able to see places that would otherwise have been impossible to see. For example, only a minority of people can travel to Egypt themselves, but thanks to photography, anyone can now see world wonders such as the pyramids with their own eyes. In addition to places, people can now look at other people as well. We have recently become completely accustomed to seeing images and footage of contemporary politicians and celebrities.

default.p.test-23-p1.vietnamese:
“Pinpon dash” refers to a children's prank: after ringing someone's doorbell with a “ding-dong,” the players turn and run away as fast as they can.

The typical image of pinpon dash is hiding nearby and watching the front door, then enjoying the sight of someone coming out with a bewildered expression, as if to say, “The doorbell clearly rang, but there's no one here.”

In reality, however, pinpon dash seems to involve ringing the bell and immediately disappearing, apparently as a way of avoiding the high-risk act of hiding and watching simply to enjoy the thrill.

In addition, pinpon dash seems to involve a desire to share the excitement and strengthen bonds among friends and companions. The people whose bells are rung have become so accustomed to it that if ① the bell rings only once, they do not open the door. That is because a single ring is most likely a sales solicitation or a pinpon-dash prank.

For example, a postal worker or home-delivery service will ring the bell two or more times. If a family member has forgotten their key, they will surely ring it repeatedly. Pinpon dash is fundamentally a game based on anticipating the target's psychology, but we have now entered an age in which that alone is no longer enough.

This is because more and more houses and neighborhoods are being equipped with security cameras. The decisive moment of a pinpon-dash prank may be captured on video. This means that ② pinpon dash is no longer a carefree, harmless game. It would be better to “graduate” from pinpon dash—that is, give it up—soon.

default.p.test-24-p1.vietnamese:
According to the Japan Vending Machine Research Institute, there are more than 4 million vending machines nationwide, or approximately one machine for every 30 people. Most vending machines are installed on streets, and the range of items that can be purchased from them is wide. In addition to cigarettes and beverages, people can buy fresh eggs, bouquets of flowers, umbrellas, men's shirts, fishing bait, tire chains, disposable cameras, and even tofu.

There is no denying that vending machines operating 24 hours a day are extremely convenient. However, the fact that they are popular even during hours when people can shop at stores may initially seem strange.

One theory is that the traditional concept of "giri"—ideas such as obligations or pressure that strangers impose on one another during transactions—still seems to exist. Transactions with machines are much more comfortable, and they are also considerably faster.

However, adding human-like features to automated devices can sometimes have the opposite effect. One beverage-vending-machine company installed a sensor on the front of its machines so that when someone approached, the machine would detect their presence and say, "Welcome," a traditional greeting used by employees when receiving customers. During the day, such machines attracted children's attention. However, late at night, people returning home alone from work on seemingly deserted streets were startled and annoyed when the machines called out to them. As a result, the "human voice" was quickly removed.

default.p.test-25-p1.vietnamese:
Starting in the new school year, new teaching and learning guidelines will be piloted at elementary and lower secondary schools, while efforts to improve the quality of moral education will also be intensified. Along with improving academic ability, moral education is the key to revitalizing public education. I hope that schools will explore and improve their teaching methods and work diligently to put this into practice.

The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology has revised ①「心のノート ("The Notebook of the Heart")」, a supplementary moral education booklet that has been distributed to all elementary and lower secondary school students. This is a comprehensive reform based on the new teaching guidelines. 「The Notebook of the Heart」was first introduced in Heisei 14 (2002), prompted by events such as the series of child-killing cases in Kobe. The book emphasizes the importance of teaching children about the preciousness of life..., while using situations from everyday life as subjects for reflection.

In the revised edition, the areas emphasized in the new teaching guidelines have been expanded and enriched, including the cultivation of an awareness of social norms, such as “following rules,” and a spirit of contributing to the community. The book also addresses recent issues, such as young people’s declining desire to work, and adds pages on the “positive meaning of work.”

Moral standards also covered in The Notebook of the Heart, such as daily greetings and the importance of helping one another..., were once naturally taught and nurtured within families and local communities. However, discipline at home is no longer being properly instilled, and the number of children who are unfamiliar with communal living from an early age is increasing. As a result, the importance of ②moral education at school is growing.

default.p.test-26-p1.vietnamese:
Whenever I want to buy a book, I usually try to visit small bookstores near my home. According to industry-wide statistics, nearly 1,000 bookstores closed down during fiscal 2006. That means that every day, two or three shops somewhere across Japan went out of business. The overwhelming majority were「neighborhood bookstores」of medium, small, or very small scale.

On the other hand, large-scale stores continue to open in urban areas. Even so, running a bookstore is far from easy because profit margins are extremely thin. The cost of goods accounts for about 80% of sales, and the remaining amount must cover personnel costs, rent, utilities, and other expenses before any profit can be made. Looking at the August 2006 financial report of the major chain Bunkyodo, sales totaled 55.27 billion yen, while operating profit was only 734 million yen. The operating margin was a mere 1.3%.

To make matters worse, shoplifting deals another painful blow. According to a survey by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, the average loss per store is approximately 2.11 million yen per year. In Bunkyodo's case alone, annual losses are estimated at 400 to 500 million yen. Preventing theft requires money and staff, and even when a thief is caught, handling the procedures takes considerable time, making this an extremely difficult problem for the business.

In this respect, selling books over the Internet saves costs and involves no shoplifters. That is why it can be profitable and has become popular. For customers, it is also extremely quick and convenient.

However, there are no unexpected encounters with books there, nor are there magical chances to stumble upon one, like in the film Notting Hill. It is dull and lacking in charm, and I feel hesitant to call it a "bookstore."

default.p.test-27-p1.vietnamese:
A

Everyone has habits that they cannot correct no matter how much they want to. Since habits are actions performed unconsciously, they can be said to reveal a person's psychology very clearly. For example, some people look upward when answering a question or thinking. People who look up to the right are often imagining scenes or objects they have never seen before, so if the other person looks this way while answering a question, one may infer that they are lying or making something up. In contrast, when people look up to the left, they are often recalling their own past experiences, so if the person being questioned makes this movement, it can be understood that they are speaking honestly. As the saying goes, "The eyes speak just as well as the mouth." Applied psychology that uses such habits can be said to have many useful applications in communication between people.

B

While dating, has your boyfriend ever suddenly started touching his nose while talking in the middle of a conversation? This is a behavior that appears when someone deliberately wants to make another person believe that something false is true. To keep this from being detected, they unconsciously touch the area around their face. The nose is located at the center of the face, so it can be regarded as symbolizing self-awareness and self-esteem. By touching it, the person is hiding their true emotions. Factors such as the other person's gestures, attitude, facial expressions, and habits can help us understand their deeper psychology. We can also apply this to the psychology of love. It may be a good idea to use this as a reference.

default.p.test-28-p1.vietnamese:
A

As everyone knows, Japan has many earthquakes. When an earthquake occurs, protecting yourself and waiting for the shaking to subside must be the top priority. In addition, after the strong shaking has eased, you should turn off and deal with sources of fire such as cooking stoves and heaters. When evacuating, turning off the circuit breaker and the main gas valve in advance will help prevent fires. The next things to do are probably to confirm that your family is safe, obtain disaster and evacuation information, secure an evacuation route, and watch out for broken glass and fallen furniture. When an earthquake occurs, people often panic and cannot make calm judgments. It is important to imagine in advance, during ordinary times, what you should do if an earthquake occurs.

B

No matter what disaster we suffer, such as a tsunami, fire, earthquake, or landslide, the most important thing is to make every effort to protect human life above all else. Among such disasters, natural disasters are something that human beings are completely powerless to prevent, no matter how much they may wish to guard against them. Although it may be possible to predict disasters, it is impossible to prevent an earthquake from occurring. If that is the case, we need to keep disaster preparedness in mind and pay attention to it during ordinary times. In addition, for several days after a disaster, essential lifelines such as tap water, gas, and telephone services will be disrupted. During those days, we must manage using our own strength. For moments like these, we need to prepare emergency necessities in advance. As the proverb says, "If you are prepared, you have nothing to fear," so we should cultivate the right mindset during ordinary times, allowing us to take appropriate action without panicking.

default.p.test-29-p1.vietnamese:
A

Propaganda is a general term for activities that use a particular ideology to influence individuals or groups and direct their actions in a predetermined direction. In particular, the term often refers to politically motivated propaganda, but it can also describe one-sided promotional activities, intensive campaigns, or indoctrination that impose particular ideas, ideologies, doctrines, or religious teachings. In short, it can be regarded as the manipulation of the masses and the shaping of public opinion through information, and is an inevitable feature of an international information society. Today, its methods do not necessarily rely on forceful imposition; they have become strategic and highly sophisticated.

Although this is a Katakana loanword that has been used for quite some time, in postwar America there was a tendency to specifically associate the word "propaganda" with Goebbels's international propaganda campaign under Nazi Germany. As a result, in Japan too the word came to evoke unpleasant feelings and was viewed with suspicion. However, from the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 through international conflicts such as the Gulf War and the Iraq War, these conflicts also became information wars involving satellite television and the Internet. The word "propaganda" therefore appears to have been reused without being limited to the narrow negative sense it once carried.

B

During World War II, the development of mass media enabled propaganda to spread ideas to much larger audiences. It is said that world leaders who had experienced World War I were keenly aware of the power of manipulating information and public psychology by making use of the media. Adolf Hitler of Nazi Germany was particularly aware of this, and promoted the Nazis' global strategy by focusing on radio broadcasting. As in Japan, Nazi propaganda during World War II had an enormous impact on society. In addition to its political aspect as an anti-communist militaristic state, Nazi propaganda advocated a brutally racist form of anti-Semitism.

default.p.test-3-p1.vietnamese: There are two types of tax investigation: 「compulsory investigations」conducted by the Inspection Department, commonly called Marusa, of the National Tax Agency, and「voluntary investigations」conducted by Regional Taxation Bureaus or Tax Offices. Compulsory investigations have strong legal authority. For example, when someone is suspected of deliberately concealing income, the Inspection Department of the National Tax Agency obtains a court warrant and searches the person’s residence. In contrast, voluntary investigations are conducted routinely to check whether tax returns are accurate through interviews and inspections of accounting books, based on the Corporation Tax Act, Income Tax Act, and other laws. After an investigation, if errors are found, the taxpayer can pay the shortfall by filing an「amended return」voluntarily, or through a「correction」made by the tax authorities using their official authority. However, if there are deliberately fraudulent secret books, the person may be criminally prosecuted and brought to court.

default.p.test-30-p1.vietnamese:
A

Universities should require students to acquire at least one foreign language, especially English. Today, countries around the world are becoming increasingly interdependent both economically and politically. If people use only the language they speak in everyday life, they may find it difficult to cope with the world situation as it is now. Even if a country thinks only of itself, it cannot develop. It cannot ignore the existence of neighboring countries. Showing a cooperative attitude is also becoming increasingly important. Therefore, mutual understanding among people from different cultural regions and with different ways of thinking is absolutely essential. The language barrier is perhaps the greatest obstacle that needs to be removed.

B

Universities should require students to acquire a second foreign language in addition to English. In essence, globalization means Americanization, and English is gradually becoming the "world's only language." It is true that wherever you go in the world, you will certainly find someone who speaks English, and acquiring such a language may be beneficial to each individual. However, is this really desirable? The world is made up of many languages and many peoples, and in order to live together in such a world, without a certain degree of linguistic diversity, it would also be difficult to understand the diversity of literature and the diversity of ideas. At university, students should study two or more foreign languages, including English.

default.p.test-31-p1.vietnamese:
A

In reality, young people’s behavior in public spaces is gradually getting worse. There are also examples that make older generations frown. For example, young women putting on makeup on trains and buses. In addition, many young people sit directly on the ground in front of convenience stores to eat or simply chat. Why has this trend spread to such an extent? The main reason is thought to be that young people today take longer than young people in the past to mature emotionally. However, responsibility does not belong only to young people themselves; it belongs to society as a whole, including the government, the education system, local communities, and families.

B

Is eating something on a train really a bad thing? It is true that it may not be desirable. However, it does not cause the people around you as much inconvenience as other troublesome behavior does. At least, it does not harm others in the same way as violence or harassment. It is simply a matter of sitting or standing there quietly while eating whatever you want. Social customs also change over time. The customs of an earlier era are not necessarily suitable for the present. Of course, this is also true of young people’s behavior in public places.

default.p.test-32-p1.vietnamese:
Person seeking advice

If your child says one morning, “I’m being bullied, so I don’t want to go to school,” how would you respond? Would you let your child stay home that day? Would you send your child to school? Or would you take your child to the school nurse’s office? Looking at it from the perspective of a sense of self-affirmation (self-esteem), I think saying “I don’t want to go” is evidence that the child is denying themself.

The child says they are being bullied because the other person’s reasoning is valid and the child has been pushed into a position where they cannot refute it. If the child could affirm themself and argue back, I do not think they would say they did not want to go to school. I feel that forcing a child who does not want to go to attend school would be meaningless. I think it is perfectly fine for the child not to go to school until they regain confidence in themself, or until an environment that allows this has been created.

Respondent A

When I was young, I complained to my mother in the same way, and she said to me, “Have you done anything wrong? If you haven’t, go to school with your head held high!” I did not miss a single day during that school year. Before long, I also made other close friends. A mother like that is probably rare. Even now, however, I can never forget my mother’s resolute attitude, and I am deeply grateful to her for it.

Respondent B

If it were me, I think I would let the child stay home for the time being. The child is hurt right now, so what would be the point of forcing them to go to school? When your child tells you, “I don’t want to go to school,” it means that they are seeking your help. Of course, you should ask the homeroom teacher or the school to verify the facts, but I hope you will treat your child’s feelings as the most important consideration.

default.p.test-33-p1.outline.0.note: The phenomenon of dogs biting their owners in real life originates in a reversal of the owner–servant relationship; socially, dogs submit to those of higher status.
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.1.label: The mistaken belief about hierarchy that leads dogs to bite their owners
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.1.note: A dog bites its owner because it mistakenly believes it is superior and views the owner as a subordinate; it bites to punish the owner when displeased or targets weaker people such as children.
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.2.label: The need to reestablish order for dogs
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.2.note: The expert advises making the dog understand that it ranks lowest in the household; without proper training, it may bite outsiders and veterinarians, endangering its own life.
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.3.label: A firm attitude and disciplined principles when training a dog
default.p.test-33-p1.outline.3.note: The key is to scold the dog firmly and decisively on the spot. Mild physical punishment may be used when necessary, but excessive violence must be avoided because it may cause the dog to bite in self-defense.

default.p.test-33-p1.vietnamese:
The expression 'being bitten by the dog one raised' is usually used to mean being betrayed by a beloved subordinate, but recently, as pet ownership has become increasingly popular, it is said that more and more people are literally being bitten by the dogs they keep. Dogs are believed to have begun living alongside humans more than 10,000 years ago. One reason humans were able to domesticate dogs is that they are social, pack-living animals that submit to those of higher status. Therefore, if the relationship with the owner is properly maintained according to a clear owner–subordinate hierarchy, a person will never be bitten by their own dog.

Conversely, dogs that bite their owners demonstrate that they believe themselves to be above humans. Because they regard the people they live with merely as servants, they bite to punish them whenever something displeases them. Some dogs never bite strangers but bare their teeth only at their owners, whom they regard as servants; in other cases, they recognize the hierarchy within the owner's family and consider only those in weaker positions, such as children, to be beneath them, targeting only those people. For this reason, pet-care and training professionals say that there is no alternative but to make the dog understand that it occupies the lowest position in the household. Some may say, 'It is too cruel to put it at the bottom,' but a dog that looks down on humans will ultimately be even more unhappy. If it becomes the kind of dog that bites people whenever it is entrusted to someone else and bites veterinary staff when taken to an animal hospital, its own life will be at risk. If you truly love your dog, you must properly train and discipline it.

The key to training is to scold the dog decisively and interact with it in a firm, clear manner. When it does something wrong, scold it immediately. At times, physical punishment, such as holding the corners of its mouth firmly with your hand or giving its nose a light smack, may also be necessary. If you approach it timidly, it will simply disregard you even when you scold it, but indiscriminate beating and intimidation are obviously not good either. The dog will become frightened and, this time, bite people out of self-defense. In addition, it is wrong to leave it merely to guard the house without playing with it or taking it for walks. Otherwise, it may bite people because it wants attention. Normally, you need to give it your undivided affection and play with it; praise is also a core part of training. Seen in this light, it is truly just like raising a child. Precisely because of love, strict discipline is sometimes the proper approach. Those who are not confident in training their dog themselves should seek out training classes or instructional seminars.

default.p.test-34-p1.vietnamese:
When I was studying abroad in Japan, ramen was one of my favorite Japanese foods. When I was in South Korea, I ate noodles only when there was nothing else to eat, when I was too lazy to cook, or when I was a little hungry. After moving to Japan, however, I somehow became “addicted” to ramen and started visiting ramen shops at least two or three times a week. I had never particularly liked ramen, so what drew me to its strange magic? First, there is the pleasure of choosing and enjoying it. Japanese ramen comes in a wide variety of flavors, such as soy sauce, miso, salt, and pork-bone broth, and the flavors are further differentiated by the noodles, broth, and toppings. Even within the same type of ramen, there are many variations, from rich and creamy to light and delicate. I never get tired of it and keep finding myself walking into ramen shops. Second, it is inexpensive and easy to enjoy. One major reason ramen has become Japan’s national dish may be its reasonable price. Side dishes that are ramen’s “close friends,” such as gyoza and fried rice, are also dependable companions that help satisfy ordinary people’s appetites alongside a bowl of ramen. Third, ramen provides considerable reassurance to people who care about “food and health.” It cannot be called a healthy dish, but depending on the type of ramen, vegetables can be added in reasonable amounts along with the carbohydrates, making it possible to continue eating it regularly.

On the other hand, some people argue that “people in Japan should limit how often they eat ramen.” Because ramen contains large amounts of carbohydrates, salt, and fat, it can easily lead to an unbalanced diet and cause lifestyle-related diseases such as obesity and high blood pressure. In addition, the Japanese habit of eating ramen to “finish off a meal” after drinking alcohol seems to be harming people’s health. Professor Nakajima of Yokohama City University Hospital explains: “When a person drinks alcohol, the liver breaks it down, consuming a large amount of blood sugar. The brain therefore sends a signal requesting carbohydrates to replenish the blood sugar, causing hunger to arise. That is why, among carbohydrate-rich foods, people especially crave ramen with lots of broth.” Eating ramen after drinking alcohol slows digestion because both alcohol and a large amount of calories are absorbed, placing a burden on the stomach and intestines. It is therefore reportedly best to switch to lighter foods such as miso soup or rice in plum-pickled-tea broth.

Even so, it is no exaggeration to call Japan a ramen paradise. Ramen shops can be found everywhere in Japan, and the ramen streets and ramen museums alone show how deeply Japanese people love ramen. Travel guidebooks invariably introduce famous ramen shops in Japan, and many devoted ramen fans tirelessly visit different shops to taste, compare, and explore them. However, I think the secret to loving something for a long time is not becoming too obsessed with it. There is a Japanese proverb that says, “You become good at what you like,” but I would say, “The more you like it, the more carefully you should take care of yourself.” For a healthy diet and balanced nutrition, I sincerely hope that everyone will be very careful not to eat too much ramen.

default.p.test-35-p1.outline.2.label: The two-sided effects of modern communication technology

default.p.test-35-p1.outline.3.label: Social challenges and the origins of negative consequences

default.p.test-35-p1.vietnamese:
Regarding ①modern science and technology, many opposing opinions have been expressed. Some people believe that science and technology are an unquestionable blessing for humanity. In other words, they believe that science and technology are the source of all progress and prosperity and will provide solutions to every social problem facing us today. Others, however, insist that science and technology bring only negative effects: taking away people's jobs, individuality, and privacy; polluting the environment; and, furthermore, causing the decline of spiritual values and the spread of materialism. Conversely, some people believe that science and technology have had less impact on society than the Industrial Revolution did, and that modern science and technology have not caused anything we cannot cope with.

Each of these opinions is correct to a certain extent, but none is entirely correct. The clearest fact concerning changes brought about by science and technology is that they produce both positive and negative effects. When science and technology create new opportunities and benefits for people and society, they simultaneously create new problems. The adoption of new opportunities and production technologies disrupts existing systems of management and employment—the established models of business and work—but on the other hand, new industries emerge, old industries are revived, and new employment opportunities appear.

②Modern communications technology has brought enormous benefits to education, commerce, and journalism. At the same time, it has also become a cause of social and international instability. This is because modern communications technology introduces foreign values「that are alien」and unsuitable for a particular society, while raising people's expectations—especially in developing countries, where those expectations cannot easily be fulfilled.

The challenge facing every modern society is to make full use of the opportunities and benefits provided by science and technology while minimizing and restraining their genuine dangers. The conflict between private and public interests often becomes the greatest obstacle to meeting this challenge. Many unwanted consequences of science and technology, such as ③pollution and social disorder, arise because businesses, both in the past and today, in many countries remain reluctant to pay for measures to prevent environmental pollution.

default.p.test-36-p1.vietnamese:
How fortunate and wonderful it is to be a reporter. I did not feel this way again until recently, when I found myself nodding in agreement with something someone else had said and felt compelled to write those words down at any cost.

The other day, on an MBS radio information program, I had the opportunity to speak with Tadao Kakizoe, honorary president of the National Cancer Center and author of the much-discussed book “Caring for My Wife at the End of Her Life” (Shinchosha). Hearing about his experiences deepened this feeling even further. He answered each call from the studio with the thought that it might help people in similar circumstances. Looking back on life after losing his beloved wife to cancer, he said, “For a while, I lived immersed in alcohol, neglecting everything and letting my life fall apart,” revealing a natural, unaffected personality throughout.

The conversation then developed as follows. After his wife died, he fell into severe depression and even considered suicide. How, then, did he find the opportunity to recover? As the conversation with the studio moved in that direction, I remembered that the writer Taku Mayumura, who had also lost his wife and continued living alone, had once written in the “New Theory of Happiness” column of our evening newspaper: “I think it is not morale that creates one's outward appearance; sometimes it is a neat outward appearance that creates morale. When people think they should try not to reveal how shabby or untidy their lives are, they manage to keep going to some extent, don't they? For example, they try not to wear shoes with worn-out soles, or think they should buy a new pair of trousers. At such times, their morale is maintained, isn't it?”

When I recounted this story, Mr. Kakizoe exclaimed, “Ah, that's absolutely true. That really does happen,” and continued as follows.

“When the shoes are polished at a shoe store and become bright and beautiful, my spirits also become orderly and uplifted. One's appearance and neatness really are extremely important, aren't they?”

As I listened, I clearly realized that he had reacted especially strongly to the words “shoes.” Thinking about it again, shoes are deeply connected with everyday life and social life through the act of walking. Without shoes, one cannot travel a long distance. If that long distance is replaced with the word “life,” shoes take on an even deeper value. The things that support our daily routines and help us continue living are, in fact, very small and simple. His words went straight to my heart and brought complete clarity to me, who had been absorbed in thinking about such matters, allowing me to empathize deeply.

The story of how, during the year and a half he and his wife struggled with illness, and even after caring for her and seeing her through her final days at home, he would still stop by a shoe store to have his leather shoes polished and thereby restore his spirits was also mentioned in his book. However, what he said on the program that day left an especially deep impression on me. Perhaps this was because, through the words that reached my ears and his genuinely plain, everyday voice, I was able to feel deeply the months and days he had lived through.

default.p.test-38-p1.vietnamese:
Fires and accidents caused by lighters have been occurring one after another. A striking number of these incidents are believed to have been caused by children playing with fire.

To prevent such tragedies from happening again, we must improve the safety of lighters while also carefully teaching children how dangerous it is to play with fire.

There have also been heartbreaking fires recently. A car fire earlier this month in Assabu, Hokkaido, killed four infants and young children, while a fire in an apartment building in Kawasaki also killed children. In both cases, the possibility that the cause originated with a lighter has emerged.

According to investigations by the Consumer Affairs Agency and the Fire and Disaster Management Agency of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, 1,319 fires caused by playing with lighters occurred in 18 government-designated cities during the five-year period from 2004 to 2008. Of these, at least approximately 40% were reportedly caused by children aged 12 or younger.

According to a survey by the National Institute of Technology and Evaluation, an independent administrative agency, 132 lighter-related accidents involving burns or clothing catching fire occurred nationwide during the five years beginning in fiscal 2004, and 9 people were seriously injured. In Kyoto Prefecture, an elderly man in his eighties with a physical disability died.

A passenger car that burned completely while traveling in Fukushima Prefecture is believed to have caught fire when the lever of a lighter that had fallen onto the floor was pressed as the power-adjustable seat was moved. There have also been many cases in which a lighter that had not been fully extinguished was accidentally put into a clothing pocket or handbag, causing a fire.

Last December, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry asked the Consumer Economics Council for its views on safety measures for lighters. A working group within the Product Safety Subcommittee is currently considering which types of lighters should be subject to regulations, as well as technical standards for features that prevent children from operating them easily.

The number of lighters in circulation domestically as of 2008 was approximately 640 million, and disposable lighters reportedly accounted for nearly 90%. Domestic products made up 12% of all lighters, while imports, including products manufactured in China, were estimated to account for as much as 88%.

In the United States and the European Union (EU), manufacturers are required to design mechanisms that prevent children from using lighters easily. In Japan, however, the matter has traditionally been left to voluntary efforts.

In Western countries, improvements have been introduced to make lighters less likely to ignite, such as requiring two or more operations before a flame can be lit or making the ignition button harder to press.

Adding safety measures will raise costs. From the consumer's perspective, this may also mean higher prices or products that are more difficult to use.

However, this is a matter of life and death. The government needs to act quickly by taking measures such as establishing safety standards.

No matter how much a product is improved, fires and accidents will still occur if it is used improperly.

Children are always curious about objects they have never seen before. It is essential to keep lighters out of children's reach. It is also important to remind parents of young children to remain vigilant.

default.p.test-4-p1.vietnamese: I was very surprised when I saw an acquaintance post on social media (SNS): 「I will no longer send New Year’s cards」. Along with New Year’s money gifts, New Year’s cards were one of the joys of the holiday season during my childhood. Whenever I looked into the mailbox on New Year’s Day, I always felt extremely excited. It is sad that New Year’s cards are gradually being replaced by social media and email. According to media reports, the number of people sending New Year’s cards continues to decline, and the number of cards delivered on New Year’s Day this year marked the eighth consecutive year of decline. It is sad that in today’s society, people casually use the excuse that they are too busy to spend a little time on a greeting card sent only once a year.

default.p.test-41-p1.vietnamese:
A classic Sichuan side dish that stimulates the appetite. Its rich flavor and mildly numbing spiciness go perfectly with plain rice. Eaten with steaming-hot rice, it leaves both body and soul feeling completely satisfied.

☀ Ingredients (serves 4)
2 blocks of tofu / 150 g ground pork / 10 g ginger / 10 g garlic / 1/2 leek
2 tablespoons cooking oil / 2 tablespoons soy sauce / 1 tablespoon cooking wine / 1 tablespoon sugar / 1 tablespoon oyster sauce
1/2 teaspoon doubanjiang / 1/2 teaspoon Chinese soup stock / 50 cc water / (Note 1) A little potato starch

☀ Key point
The key to stir-frying is to work quickly over high heat. To do this, prepare all the ingredients in advance. In addition, briefly boiling the tofu first allows some of the water inside it to escape, making it less likely to crumble. When turning the tofu, use broad movements from the bottom upward and be careful not to break it apart.

☀ Directions
① Cut the tofu into bite-sized pieces; mince the garlic, ginger, and leek in advance.
② Gently boil the 2 blocks of tofu in boiling water for about 1 minute, then remove and drain.
③ Heat a pan thoroughly, add the cooking oil, stir-fry the garlic, ginger, and leek first, and then add the doubanjiang.
④ When the garlic and ginger become fragrant, add the ground pork and stir-fry thoroughly so that the heat cooks it all the way through.
⑤ Once the meat has been thoroughly stir-fried and changes color, add the soy sauce, cooking wine, sugar, and oyster sauce, and mix well.
⑥ Add the tofu, Chinese soup stock, and water, then simmer over medium heat for about 2 minutes so that some of the liquid evaporates and the flavors are absorbed.
⑦ Dissolve the potato starch in water, pour it in, and stir until the sauce thickens.

default.p.test-45-p10.outline.4.label: A lesson on freeing organizations from stagnation
default.p.test-45-p10.outline.4.note: The proposed solution to breaking through prejudice and resignation within an organization is to introduce a new factor—new personnel—which conveys the author's central message.
default.p.test-45-p10.vietnamese:
Barracuda are aggressive fish that are sometimes said to attack humans as well. When discussing businesses or organizations, what frequently comes up is ① the “Barracuda Theory,” which focuses on this fish's behavior.

A barracuda is released into a tank, and small fish are thrown in as prey. It immediately rushes at them with its sharp teeth. Next, a transparent partition is placed in the tank, with the barracuda on one side and the small fish on the other. The barracuda repeatedly hurls its body against the partition in an attempt to eat the prey, but cannot do so. Eventually, it gives up, and it is said that even after the partition is removed, it no longer bothers to attack the small fish.

In an experiment conducted by the psychologist Seligman, dogs were subjected to electric shocks. At first, the dogs ran around trying to escape, but despite their movements, the shocks continued at regular intervals. After a while, the dogs stopped running around and began enduring the shocks until the unpleasant stimulus subsided. The same principle applies to circus elephants that do not run away even when restrained by a single thin rope. Since they were chained with a thick, sturdy chain when they were young, they learn that although they become strong enough as adults to pull up the stake and break the rope whenever they wish, they still do not do so. Both the dogs and the elephants have learned to give up.

The same thing happens in human society. When repeated efforts have no effect whatsoever on the surrounding environment, psychology calls the act of stopping those efforts and giving up ② “learned helplessness.” Akiteru Teramoto, chief consultant at the Hamagin Research Institute, has pointed out: “Apathy and powerlessness are contagious. What is frightening is that an experience learned by one individual does not merely spread within that individual; it also affects people who have never experienced it themselves through indirect, vicarious experience, negatively influencing corporate culture.”

When demand declines and the market shrinks, an atmosphere of resignation begins to spread. Even when carefully developed new product plans or sales methods are proposed, people tend to search from the outset for reasons they cannot be implemented or excuses for not carrying them out. Once the sense of powerlessness expressed by the thought “Nothing will do any good” has spread everywhere, the company has no future.

The “Barracuda Theory” has a further part. After the partition has been removed, another barracuda is released into the tank. Naturally, the newly introduced barracuda rushes toward the small fish. On seeing this, the original barracuda reportedly seems to wake up and also launches a fierce attack on the small fish.

When an organization becomes stagnant, it is easy for “partitions” leading to mistaken assumptions and resignation to form. Bringing in a new barracuda may be an effective way to remove those barriers and reactivate the organization's energy. The spring personnel-transfer season is an excellent opportunity to awaken barracuda that have stopped pursuing the small fish.

Since the headquarters allows franchisees to use its brand, they do not need to advertise and receive support from purchasing through sales. They are also taught business techniques, from choosing a location to managing operations, so even people without experience can feel very secure. In return, the business operator must pay royalties, such as a franchise joining fee and a percentage of sales; that is how this system works. default.p.test-45-p3.outline.3.label: The intensity of idol fandom in the past and today

default.p.test-45-p3.vietnamese: It was around the time when only about a week remained before the end of summer vacation. I sat at the low round table in my room and groaned over the pile of homework I had foolishly allowed to accumulate. Every year was the same: although I set a goal of finishing everything during July, I was the kind of person who could not resist immediate pleasures, and I had never once managed to do it. I worked fairly diligently during the first week or so, but as soon as I had a little free time, I became careless and gave priority to playing. I still had not corrected that bad habit even after entering junior high school, and as a result, I was suffering just as I did every year. In the next room, my mother was, as usual, sewing diligently while listening to the radio. The wind chime hanging by the window did not make even a single sound, and then Masaaki Hirao's song 'The Star That Knows Everything' began to play, causing me to stop my pencil without thinking. Young girls are still devoted to idols today, and things were similar back then. In fact, considering the level of enthusiasm, it may have been even more intense in the past.

default.p.test-45-p4.vietnamese: Why do Japanese people love cherry blossoms so deeply? From mid-March to early April, famous cherry-blossom-viewing spots throughout Japan become crowded with people enjoying the flowers. It is also common to see groups of family members, friends, or coworkers gathering together, happily chatting over boxed lunches. In a country like Japan, where the four seasons are clearly defined, the blooming of cherry blossoms signals the arrival of spring and brings hope for a new life. In addition, the Japanese people's special affection for cherry blossoms is thought to be connected to a Buddhist idea known as「the view of impermanence」.「The view of impermanence」is the belief that nothing in this world remains unchanged and that everything is constantly transforming. default.p.test-45-p5.vietnamese: I have loved movies since childhood. American films from the period immediately after the war had a somewhat special meaning for me. In addition to the appeal of the stories, the beauty of the actresses, and the actors' talent, the things shown on the screen were incredibly unfamiliar and wonderful, making me feel as though I were catching a glimpse of a dream world. If you ask what seemed dreamlike, it was electric refrigerators, electric vacuum cleaners, and toasters. Since we had never seen such things, even when a film portrayed an ordinary family, I felt as though I were looking at a magnificent palace. I think I watched movies back then with countless misconceptions. The logo shown at the beginning of each film was a symbol of that dream. MGM films showed a roaring lion. Paramount films showed shining stars above a mountain. Universal films showed a rotating globe. 20th Century Fox films showed searchlights sweeping across the sky. Whenever the logo appeared, I felt tremendously excited and thrilled.

default.p.test-45-p6.vietnamese:
The “Premium Friday” campaign—calling on people to finish work at 3 p.m. on the last Friday of each month so they can enjoy shopping and travel—is about to begin. This movement was launched by the government and the Japan Business Federation (Keidanren) with the aim of stimulating consumer demand and promoting work-style reform. In reality, however, many people may find it difficult to leave work early. Some also argue that its effect on expanding consumption will be limited. I hope that the government and businesses will use this opportunity to create an environment in which workers can take time off more easily.

The model was the United States' year-end “Black Friday” sales event, which has a proven track record of stimulating and boosting consumption. The number of businesses and organizations offering products and services for Premium Friday has surpassed 3,000. Restaurants are opening earlier, and travel companies are preparing packages that allow guests to check in late on Friday evening. Everyone is looking forward to a business opportunity.

However, in today's climate of stagnant incomes, having more free time alone is unlikely to raise overall consumption. If people spend money on Friday and cut back on Saturday, there is a serious risk that this will simply mean bringing future demand forward. If the goal is to expand consumption, the proper course is to focus efforts on raising wages, including improving benefits for non-regular workers. Meanwhile, businesses that allow employees to leave early have not yet become widespread.

Keidanren has called on its member companies to let employees leave early, and some major corporations have agreed to move up starting times by encouraging employees to use annual leave or introducing flextime systems. Nevertheless, many companies maintain normal working hours in order to prioritize relationships with business partners and serve customers. Some also argue that ending work early would merely increase overtime or require employees to work on holidays on other days. If so, that would completely defeat the purpose. Employees of small and medium-sized businesses—which account for as much as 70% of all businesses—are expected to find it even more difficult to leave early. This is because labor shortages have prevented systems that allow everyone to take time off from being fully established.

default.p.test-45-p7.vietnamese:
Although we were confident in both the quality and price of our products for export, sales were inexplicably poor. We sent local investigators to mix our products with those of other companies believed to be competitors and conduct blind tests. Contrary to expectations, our company's products received better evaluations. Yet they did not sell at all.

The investigators went into markets, approached local people who were choosing competing products, and tactfully asked why they did not buy our product instead. To our great surprise, the answer was: "Because it has a sun symbol on it."

In Japan, images such as the morning sun, dawn, the sun, and the red sun on the national flag are very popular in product names and are also widely used in brand names and designs. However, for people from cultures that have lived in deserts year-round and suffered from the scorching heat of the sun, the sun is not the source of life and beneficence that Japanese people believe it to be; it is a cursed presence that can mean death after even the slightest mistake.

The positive feelings Japanese people associate almost religiously with concepts such as "the first sunrise of the year," "sunlight shining on a mountaintop," and "the sun god" are completely incomprehensible to Arabs. For them, when such a frightening and taboo presence becomes a food brand, it represents nothing but an extremely negative and unpleasant image.

If Arabs hate the sun so much, then what celestial body do they love? It is the moon. When the terrifying sun that turns the world into a sea of burning sand and scorches everything finally sets, the desert suddenly becomes cool. People regain their vitality and finally feel reborn. The aesthetics of the moon, in which the moon represents beauty, salvation, and hope, arose from precisely this setting. That is why, in Islamic civilization rooted in Arab culture, the moon—and especially the crescent moon—is so highly honored and praised. This is also why nine countries that have Islam as their state religion or a major religion currently feature the crescent moon on their national flags.

default.p.test-45-p8.vietnamese:
As globalization progresses worldwide, opportunities to encounter different cultures and peoples are increasing rapidly. Many studies have been reported examining issues that arise as cultures move, come into contact, and interact with one another.

Berry focused on intercultural stress and the acculturation of individuals living in a cultural environment different from that of their home country. Based on this, he proposed a theory of acculturation called “acculturation strategies.” Acculturation strategies are the attitudes, behaviors, and coping methods that an individual living between their own culture and another culture may choose. They express the degree of attachment the individual feels toward their original culture and the adopted culture.

Berry proposed four patterns—“integration,” “assimilation,” “separation,” and “marginalization”—from two perspectives: “Should one value the local culture and build new relationships with it?” and “Should one maintain one's original culture?”

Integration: The most positive attitude toward another culture; valuing and accepting both cultures. This is a pattern in which the two cultures coexist.
Assimilation: Rejecting one's own culture and gradually adapting to the other culture.
Separation: Valuing only one's own culture and rejecting the other culture.
Marginalization: Failing to integrate into either culture.

Berry's analysis was innovative because it focused not only on the process by which individuals gradually adapt to another culture, but also on preserving and developing their own cultural identity. Another difference from earlier research is that it clearly identifies and describes the characteristics of each pattern. However, although the four patterns above help reveal certain tendencies toward one's own culture and other cultures, they are limited in that they do not address people who do not fit any of these patterns.

default.p.test-45-p9.vietnamese:
A
In Japan today, the proportion of single-person households is steadily rising compared with that of family households. In other words, the number of people belonging to the "Ohitorisama" (people who live alone) group is increasing. Some Ohitorisama live independently, enjoying hobbies and private time on their own, arranging their living situation, and preparing for old age. However, some people may have become Ohitorisama unwillingly. Among them, many begin to feel anxious when they see friends around them getting married one after another, and start looking for a marriage partner through "Konkatsu." Konkatsu is a shortened term for activities related to marriage: searching for a suitable partner based on one's own conditions in the hope of having a happy marriage. Konkatsu is not limited to going on arranged dates; it includes a wide range of activities, such as visiting beauty salons, taking cooking classes, going to the gym, and dieting. Recently, Konkatsu has also become an industry, with businesses creating places for people to meet, such as matchmaking parties.

B
The Ministry of Health predicts that, among men aged 30 and over, one in three, and among women, one in five, will reach old age without ever marrying. Against this background, some people have pointed out that the belief that "marriage is something one must do" is gradually disappearing. The idea that choosing not to marry is a matter of personal freedom is becoming increasingly widespread. Reasons why men do not marry include having no opportunities to meet someone, low income, and finding it more comfortable to live alone. On the other hand, many women say that living with someone else is troublesome, that they have not met a suitable person, and that the freedom of living alone is important. Reflecting this kind of Japanese society, the term "Ohitorisama" was also coined. Companies are now actively developing services for Ohitorisama, including travel, dining, and moviegoing services. This shows that society is accepting the Ohitorisama lifestyle. In the future, demand for Ohitorisama services will probably continue to increase.

default.p.test-46-p10.vietnamese:
To reduce greenhouse-gas emissions on campus, Mie University in Tsu will launch a carbon-offset initiative that offsets the carbon dioxide (CO₂) emitted on campus against reductions in CO₂ emissions achieved in the homes of students, faculty, and staff.

In exchange for awarding eco points for reductions in household CO₂ emissions, the university will count those reductions toward the university-wide total. According to Japan’s Ministry of the Environment, CO₂-reduction trading is common among businesses, while trading reductions achieved by households is a rare experiment. The university will begin a trial this autumn and launch the program officially in conjunction with the introduction, from April of the following year, of IC chips for student and staff ID cards incorporating prepaid electronic money.

Under the Energy Conservation Act, the university works every year to reduce CO₂ emissions. In November of the previous year, with the aim of achieving further reductions, it established an energy-conservation planning committee consisting of professors, a gas company, and representatives from supermarkets. The university formulated a medium- and long-term plan extending through fiscal 2020.

Under the plan, the university aims to reduce emissions by 30% in fiscal 2020 compared with fiscal 1990 through measures such as conserving electricity on campus and installing state-of-the-art energy-saving equipment. It has included the adoption of carbon offsetting as part of this policy. The university has also decided to seek cooperation from alumni and local residents, and is considering whether eco points could be used at supermarkets outside the campus in addition to the student cooperative (COOP) and convenience stores on campus.

Specific details, such as the conversion rate for eco points, will be decided later. For example, if a reduction in consumption from the previous year is confirmed based on itemized electricity, gas, and water bills after a student makes efforts to conserve energy at home, the university will award eco points corresponding to the reduction.

Assuming that approximately 6,000 people, equivalent to half the students and alumni, participate, the university expects to achieve a reduction of 3.2%, equivalent to 1/10 (10%) of its reduction target (30%). If each kilogram of CO₂ is converted into 2 yen for students and 1 yen for alumni, the annual cost of the eco points is estimated at approximately ¥4 million, which the university will cover in full.

The university is also adding an eco-point function to the IC-chip student ID card to improve its convenience. In addition, regarding electronic money, it is considering becoming the first university to issue a student ID card compatible with the Aeon Group’s WAON electronic wallet.

University President Atsumasa Uchida, who aims to make the university one of the world’s leading advanced environmental universities, said: “We can provide students with practical environmental education. Furthermore, if efforts to reduce CO₂ centered on Mie University spread throughout the local community, this will also lead to a change in how students and residents perceive environmental issues.”

default.p.test-46-p4.vietnamese:

default.p.test-46-p6.vietnamese:
A bicycle shop in Fukuoka displays a jumble of bicycles and rusty parts. A few days ago, I bought a refurbished bicycle there. The rust had been polished away, and the bicycle rides very smoothly.

The streets of Fukuoka are filled with bicycles abandoned carelessly. According to the city authorities, more than 50,000 bicycles were removed and impounded during fiscal 2005. This number has been increasing every year. Less than 40% of the bicycles were identified and returned to their owners. More than half were discarded and destroyed, while the remaining 10% were sold to businesses or reused at welfare facilities. The bicycle I bought was one of those that had been “brought back to life” after being impounded.

If a bicycle is left in a no-parking area, it will be impounded after only a short time. “I locked it carefully to look after it. This was not an abandoned bicycle. Taking it without permission is theft!” Apparently, some people angrily make complaints like this to the officials in charge at the ward office.

Although bicycle parking areas have been planned and improved, many cyclists still refuse to use them. On the other hand, pedestrians sometimes feel uneasy about bicycles speeding along the sidewalks. For these reasons, the negative aspects tend to be emphasized and scrutinized.

However, many European countries encourage bicycles as an environmentally friendly means of transportation and have established dedicated bicycle lanes. To gain the understanding and support of city residents, cyclists themselves must first develop greater awareness of proper civic behavior. I thought this as I rode my bicycle.

default.p.test-46-p7.vietnamese:
A woman I know complained, “Ugh, I’ve lost another umbrella. Someone must have taken it.” Apparently, she had left it in a taxi while going home late at night. She contacted the taxi company the next morning, but in the end, it was never found.

When I asked her about it, I learned that over the past few years she had lost two umbrellas in taxis, including this one, one on a train, and one at a hospital. One had also disappeared from the umbrella stand at her workplace. She angrily said, “I bought all five because I really liked them. For now, I’ll just use 500-yen plastic umbrellas.”

Here is some statistical data. According to the Lost and Found Center of the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department, 427,655 umbrellas were reported as found property in Tokyo over the past year. By contrast, only 2,791 umbrellas were reported as lost. Umbrellas have entered the age of single use and disposal. Perhaps that is why, even when someone leaves an umbrella in a taxi or on a train, people can casually “borrow” it without giving it much thought.

Even when I look at my own habits, I have as many as four plastic umbrellas at home. Although I worry that it might rain, I often go out without an umbrella, thinking that I can simply buy one if it does. In the past, I used to write my name on an umbrella and take good care of it for many years. It may be only an umbrella, but sometimes it makes us stop and reconsider our behavior.【Hiroaki Goto】

default.p.test-46-p8.outline.0.note: The author defines “experience” and illustrates it through overseas travel: taking an all-inclusive tour does not necessarily make someone an experienced traveler.

default.p.test-46-p8.outline.1.note: For an experience to become experience-based expertise, knowledge and techniques are necessary; the discussion expands to the example of giving birth and becoming a parent.
default.p.test-46-p8.outline.2.label: The experience of becoming a parent and understanding one's own parents
default.p.test-46-p8.outline.2.note: Having a child is only an “experience of becoming a parent”; raising a child helps people understand what their own parents felt in the past.
default.p.test-46-p8.outline.3.label: Experience and practical knowledge concerning children and parents.
default.p.test-46-p8.outline.3.note: The passage concludes with a paradox: raising a child is when one gains 'experience as a child,' while 'experience as a parent' comes only after understanding one's own child—often when the child has already grown up.
default.p.test-46-p8.vietnamese:
Experience means personally seeing, hearing, touching, or trying something oneself. Thus, for example, anyone can become someone with overseas travel experience simply by traveling abroad. However, that alone is not enough to proudly call oneself experienced in overseas travel. Even if someone has traveled abroad, if it was a carefully arranged package tour that took care of everything from A to Z, they could complete the trip without even needing to know how to buy tickets, go through immigration and customs, or check into a hotel. Things are different on an independent trip or a honeymoon where only the married couple travel together. If you cannot manage anything on your own, your bride may end up becoming fed up with you.

When we speak of ① experience, merely trying or experiencing something oneself is not enough; one must also grasp something intellectually meaningful from it. Once thrown into a real-world situation, even if one dislikes it, one must learn the specialized know-how necessary to survive and work there. When that happens, experience becomes expertise. Of course, there are also times when this does not happen. Getting married and having children can make someone a parent. No—even without getting married, someone can still become a parent.

However, at this stage, it is still merely the ② experience of being a parent. Thinking it over carefully, I realized that what remains at the stage of experience is not only "oneself in the role of a parent"; "oneself in the role of a child" seems to be the same way. Someone once said that raising children is what finally enables people to fully understand how their own parents felt when they were young.

It is only at that point that people can understand what feelings their parents had when raising them in their childhood. This means that it takes many years afterward to truly "gain experience as oneself in the role of a child." People experience being a child and grow into adults, and while experiencing parenthood, they finally "gain experience as a child." If so, when does one truly "gain experience as a parent"? Perhaps it is the moment when one understands the thoughts and feelings of one's own child. Yet in most cases, by the time one has accumulated enough experience as a parent and learned the know-how of raising children, the child-rearing period has already come to an end.

default.p.test-46-p9.vietnamese:
Person Seeking Advice
I live in an apartment complex that does not allow pets. In the past, trouble caused by one family who kept a cat led the complex to ban pets. Since dogs and cats that had already been kept could not simply be abandoned, they were temporarily allowed, but keeping new pets has been prohibited. However, judging from their ages and even their faces, it is obvious that some residents are acquiring new pets. ①People like that angrily argue back, "Your family is keeping one too... Now that things have gone this far, are you really telling us to throw it away?" In the end, my daughter could not stand it any longer and started asking to keep a pet. Is there any way I can persuade her?

Respondent A
I am allergic to cats. I love animals and, of course, I love cats too, but whenever I am around one, I start coughing, sneezing, and having a runny nose, and within a few hours I develop a fever and collapse. Apparently, some people even die from allergies. Why not tell your daughter that you are allergic to cats? Teaching children that some things simply have to be accepted is also part of a parent's education, isn't it?

Respondent B
I also love animals, so I understand your daughter's feelings painfully well. Rules are supposed to be followed, but considering the actual situation, I think some things are impossible no matter what. Adults openly break the rules too, so I suppose it cannot be helped. Please fulfill your daughter's wish.
